taxa.name: Life (LUCA lineage)
taxa.note: Earliest widely accepted fossils (stromatolites) about 3.48 Ga; molecular-clock estimates put the last universal common ancestor near 4.2 Ga.

taxa.name: Eukaryota
taxa.note: Placed inside the archaeal branch, as most recent analyses do.

taxa.name: Archaeplastida
taxa.note: Bangiomorpha, a red alga, about 1.05 Ga.

taxa.name: Embryophyta
taxa.note: Oldest spores about 470 Ma; molecular clocks somewhat older.

taxa.name: Fungi
taxa.note: Ourasphaira, about 0.9 to 1.0 Ga.

taxa.name: Metazoa
taxa.note: Dickinsonia about 558 Ma; older biomarker claims are debated, hence the wide range.

taxa.name: Trilobita
taxa.note: Present for almost 270 million years; the last disappear at the end-Permian extinction.

taxa.name: Ammonoidea
taxa.note: Survived three of the Big Five, not the fourth one they met.

taxa.name: Vertebrata
taxa.note: Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, Chengjiang biota, about 518 Ma.

taxa.name: Conodonta
taxa.note: Eel-like early vertebrates known mostly from their teeth; gone at the end-Triassic extinction.

taxa.name: Placodermi
taxa.note: The dominant Devonian vertebrates; the last vanish at the end of the Devonian.

taxa.name: Osteichthyes
taxa.note: Guiyu, about 423 Ma.

taxa.name: Tetrapoda
taxa.note: Trackways about 395 Ma; Ichthyostega bodies about 365 Ma.

taxa.name: Amniota
taxa.note: Hylonomus, about 318 Ma.

taxa.name: Gorgonopsia
taxa.note: Sabre-toothed top predators of the late Permian.

taxa.name: Mammalia
taxa.note: Crown mammals; mammal-like mammaliaforms go back to about 205 Ma.

taxa.name: Primates
taxa.note: Purgatorius, within about 100,000 years of the K-Pg boundary.

taxa.name: Homo sapiens
taxa.note: Jebel Irhoud, about 315,000 years ago.

taxa.name: Ichthyosauria
taxa.note: Gone about 28 million years before the K-Pg impact: not every Mesozoic reptile died with the dinosaurs.

taxa.name: Dinosauria
taxa.note: Unambiguous dinosaurs about 231 Ma; Nyasasaurus, about 243 Ma, may be one. Still living, as birds.

taxa.name: Ornithischia
taxa.note: Triassic members are debated, hence the wide range.

taxa.name: Theropoda
taxa.note: Still living, as birds.

taxa.name: Dromaeosauridae
taxa.note: Teeth may extend the record to about 167 Ma; skeletons from about 125 Ma.

taxa.name: Paraves
taxa.note: Anchiornis, about 160 Ma.

taxa.name: Enantiornithes
taxa.note: The most diverse Cretaceous birds, wiped out at the boundary.

taxa.name: Aves (Neornithes)
taxa.note: Asteriornis, 66.7 Ma, is the oldest well-dated crown bird.

taxa.name: Sphenisciformes
taxa.note: Waimanu, about 61 Ma.

taxa.name: Passer domesticus
taxa.note: The species' fossil record is short and uncertain; the range is deliberately wide.

extinctions.name: End-Ordovician
extinctions.durationNote: two pulses within the Hirnantian stage
extinctions.description: Glaciation and sea-level fall, then warming; marine invertebrates hit hardest.

extinctions.name: Late Devonian
extinctions.durationNote: a series of pulses, chiefly the Kellwasser (~372 Ma) and Hangenberg (~359 Ma) events
extinctions.description: Reef ecosystems collapse; the armoured placoderms disappear by the end.

extinctions.name: End-Permian
extinctions.description: The largest: Siberian Traps volcanism, warming and ocean acidification. Trilobites end here.

extinctions.name: End-Triassic
extinctions.durationNote: tied to the onset of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province
extinctions.description: Clears the way for dinosaurs to dominate the Jurassic. Conodonts end here.

extinctions.name: Cretaceous–Paleogene (K-Pg)
extinctions.durationNote: the Chicxulub impact at 66.04 Ma; ecosystem collapse within about 30,000 years
extinctions.description: Non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, plesiosaurs, mosasaurs and ammonites vanish; crown birds and mammals survive.

tours.title: From the first cells to a sparrow

steps.caption: 4.5 billion years ago: a molten, barren Earth. No life yet.
By 3.48 billion years ago, microbial mats leave the oldest widely accepted fossils.
Animals appear before the Cambrian; within a few million years most body plans are in the record.
The Jurassic: dinosaurs dominate on land, pterosaurs in the air.
Theropods: one branch of them leads to Archaeopteryx and the birds.
66 million years ago: the K-Pg impact. Every non-avian dinosaur lineage ends; crown birds survive.
A house sparrow today: its ancestry runs back through the theropods to the first cells.
